text: This morning, you probably did something without even thinking about it.
You picked up a plastic stick, squeezed some paste onto it, and scrubbed your teeth.
Two minutes. Done.
But plastic toothbrushes are less than a hundred years old.
So for almost all of human history, what did people do?
Rewind fourteen thousand years.
Strangely, most early hunter-gatherers had surprisingly few cavities.
Their food was tough and chewy, with almost no sugar.
Then humans started farming.
Bread. Porridge. Grain, all day long.
And cavities shot up.
Now people had a problem they could not ignore. Toothache.
And here's the part most people don't know.
In a rock shelter in northern Italy, scientists found a fourteen-thousand-year-old tooth.
Inside its cavity were tiny scratch marks. Someone had scraped out the rot with a sharp stone tool.
It's one of the oldest known signs of dentistry.
In Slovenia, a sixty-five-hundred-year-old tooth turned up with its crack sealed with beeswax.
A filling. Made of wax.
But what about cleaning?
The simplest answer was a twig.
People chewed the end of a stick until it frayed into a soft little brush.
In India it's called datun, often cut from a neem tree. In the Middle East, it's miswak.
Millions of people still use them today.
The ancient Egyptians went further. They ground eggshells, ash and myrrh into a powder. An early toothpaste.
But people got one big thing wrong.
For thousands of years, from Babylon to medieval Europe, many believed toothache was caused by a tiny worm, eating the tooth from inside.
There was no worm. It was bacteria.
Then, in fourteen ninety-eight, in China, someone fixed stiff hog bristles into a handle of bone or bamboo. The first bristle toothbrush.
Around seventeen eighty, an Englishman named William Addis made one in prison, from a small bone and some bristles, and later sold them across Britain.
And in nineteen thirty-eight, nylon replaced the hog hair.
So the next time you brush, remember.
That little plastic stick is the latest weapon in a fourteen-thousand-year fight against an enemy you can't even see.
